\section{Overview}

Declarations of the Lean module \texttt{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist}.

\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Finite probability distribution]
\lean{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist}
\statementsource{Vad12}{pdf-bf2ce5422088-p011-b003}
\statementsource{HILL99}{pdf-130039751e9f-p007-b002}
\label{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist}
\leanok
A finite probability distribution on a finite set $\alpha$ assigns a real number $p(a)$
to each $a\in\alpha$, with $p(a)\ge 0$ for every $a$ and $\sum_{a\in\alpha}p(a)=1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Evaluation of a constructed distribution]
\lean{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.coe_mk}
\label{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.coe_mk}
\leanok
\uses{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist}
\difficulty{1}
Let $\alpha$ be a finite type, and let $f:\alpha\to\bbr$ be nonnegative at every outcome
and have total sum $1$. For every $a\in\alpha$, the probability assigned to $a$ by the
distribution constructed from $f$ is $f(a)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Extensionality of finite distributions]
\lean{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.ext}
\label{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.ext}
\leanok
\uses{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist}
\difficulty{4}
Let $p$ and $q$ be probability distributions on the same finite set. If they assign the
same probability to every outcome, then $p=q$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Probability of an Outcome]
\lean{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.le_one}
\label{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.le_one}
\leanok
\uses{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist}
\difficulty{3}
Let $p$ be a probability distribution on a finite set $\alpha$. For every $a\in\alpha$,
the probability $p(a)$ is at most $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Nonempty outcome set]
\lean{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.card_pos}
\label{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.card_pos}
\leanok
\uses{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist}
\difficulty{4}
If a finite set $\alpha$ is equipped with a probability distribution, then $\alpha$ is nonempty;
equivalently, its cardinality is positive.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Uniform distribution]
\lean{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.uniform}
\statementsource{Vad12}{pdf-bf2ce5422088-p011-b003}
\statementsource{HILL99}{pdf-130039751e9f-p007-b002}
\statementsource{CW79}{pdf-1c24478649f7-p004-b002}
\label{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.uniform}
\leanok
\uses{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist}
For a nonempty finite set $\alpha$, define the uniform probability distribution by
assigning probability $1/|\alpha|$ to each element of $\alpha$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Distribution under a map]
\lean{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.map}
\statementsource{HILL99}{pdf-130039751e9f-p007-b002}
\label{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.map}
\leanok
\uses{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist}
Given finite sets $\alpha$ and $\beta$, a function $f:\alpha\to\beta$, and a probability
distribution $p$ on $\alpha$, define the distribution of $f(a)$ when $a$ is sampled
according to $p$ by assigning to each $b\in\beta$ the probability
$\sum_{a\in\alpha:f(a)=b}p(a)$.
\end{definition}

\difficulty{1}
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be finite sets, let $p$ be a probability distribution on
$\alpha$, and let $f\colon\alpha\to\beta$. For every $b\in\beta$, the probability
assigned to $b$ by the distribution induced by $f$ is $\sum_{a\in\alpha:\,f(a)=b}p(a)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Product distribution]
\lean{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.prod}
\statementsource{HILL99}{
  pdf-130039751e9f-p007-b002,
  pdf-130039751e9f-p011-b001
}
\label{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.prod}
\leanok
\uses{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist}
Given probability distributions $p$ and $q$ on finite sets $\alpha$ and $\beta$,
respectively, define their product distribution on $\alpha\times\beta$ by assigning
$(a,b)$ probability $p(a)q(b)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Product Distribution Probability]
\lean{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.prod_apply}
\label{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.prod_apply}
\leanok
\uses{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist, TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.prod}
\difficulty{1}
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be finite sets, and let $p$ and $q$ be probability
distributions on them, respectively. The product distribution assigns probability
$p(a)q(b)$ to each pair $(a,b)\in\alpha\times\beta$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Collision probability]
\lean{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.collision}
\statementsource{Vad12}{
  pdf-bf2ce5422088-p088-b005,
  pdf-bf2ce5422088-p174-b004
}
\statementsource{HILL99}{pdf-130039751e9f-p008-b002}
\label{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.collision}
\leanok
\uses{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist}
For a probability distribution $p$ on a finite set $\alpha$, define its collision
probability to be $\sum_{a\in\alpha}p(a)^2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Nonnegativity of collision probability]
\lean{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.collision_nonneg}
\label{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.collision_nonneg}
\leanok
\uses{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist, TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.collision}
\difficulty{1}
For every probability distribution $p$ on a finite set, its collision probability $\sum_a
p(a)^2$ is nonnegative.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Collision probability of the uniform distribution]
\lean{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.collision_uniform}
\label{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.collision_uniform}
\leanok
\uses{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.collision, TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.uniform, TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.uniform_apply}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\alpha$ be a nonempty finite set, and give each of its elements equal probability. The
collision probability of this uniform distribution is the reciprocal of the cardinality
of $\alpha$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Lower bound on collision probability]
\lean{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.inv_card_le_collision}
\label{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.inv_card_le_collision}
\leanok
\uses{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist, TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.card_pos, TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.collision}
\difficulty{4}
For every probability distribution $p$ on a finite set $\alpha$, its collision probability
$\sum_a p(a)^2$ is at least the reciprocal of the cardinality of $\alpha$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Min-entropy bound]
\lean{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.HasMinEntropy}
\statementsource{Vad12}{
  pdf-bf2ce5422088-p176-b001,
  pdf-bf2ce5422088-p206-b001,
  pdf-bf2ce5422088-p209-b002
}
\label{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.HasMinEntropy}
\leanok
\uses{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist}
A probability distribution $p$ on a finite set $\alpha$ has min-entropy at least
$k\in\mathbb R$ if $p(a)\le 2^{-k}$ for every $a\in\alpha$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Collision probability under a min-entropy bound]
\lean{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.collision_le_of_hasMinEntropy}
\label{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.collision_le_of_hasMinEntropy}
\leanok
\uses{TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist, TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.HasMinEntropy, TCSlib.InformationTheory.FinDist.collision}
\difficulty{3}
Let $p$ be a probability distribution on a finite set and let $k\in\mathbb R$. If every outcome
has probability at most $2^{-k}$, then the collision probability $\sum_a p(a)^2$ is at most
$2^{-k}$.
\end{theorem}
